utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: First I would like to give the Chamber's decision in relation to a Defence submission. On the 11th of June, the Chamber deferred its decision on the request for protective measures for three Defence witnesses until such time as the Defence was able to provide supplementing information, supporting the request. On the 18th of June that information was provided. The Prosecution has no objection to the Chamber granting the requested protective measures. In light of all the circumstances, including the additional information provided by the Defence and also in light of the relevant provisions of the Statute and the Rules, the Chamber grants the motion and orders that witnesses T-5, T-24, and T-54 testify using a pseudonym and with image distortion. The reference to Witness T-54 should have been T-44. So much for that matter. The next matter I wish to raise was the oral motion made yesterday by the Defence for use of the Sarajevo field offices, and I ask whether any consultation has taken place between the parties about this matter in light of the submissions made by the Prosecutor. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We cooperated with the Prosecutor and with Mr. Hogan, the investigator at OTP. We're starting to collect useful information in order to be able to use the field office in Belgrade and in Sarajevo. However, what will be really useful for Defence is that the Victims and Witnesses Section follow-up on this cooperation. There are four witnesses involved who are living either outside Sarajevo or Belgrade and to make sure that they can be here on time at the scheduled time and day, Defence would like to obtain help from the Victims and Witnesses Section. We made a request to the section and we were told that we would have an answer in writing, but as of now we don't know yet what the section is going to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But evidently, you have made some progress in relation to the -- in relation to your requests? You are able to use the field office? Is this matter that is outstanding relating to the Victims and Witnesses Unit?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, regarding the premises, we were told that it was going to be okay. However, we've -- we have contacted the witnesses last week and Defence wanted to go over there during the week of June 25, but it's been postponed by a week now. And we're still waiting and we're going to have to tell witnesses about the change in dates. We -- we absolutely need help from the Witnesses and Victims Section because the witnesses will only have to go to Belgrade or Sarajevo instead of having to go all the way to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question then, Ms. Isailovic, is whether the motion still remains live or is it now moot?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it is because we haven't received an answer from the Witnesses -- and Witnesses Section yet. I don't really know what kind of ruling or decisions could be useful to make sure that they help us. Otherwise, you know, we can have all the witness -- all the premises available, but if we cannot move the witnesses to the premises, it would be useless. We need to have the witnesses there on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple of points. First of all, the field office told me they weren't aware of any request by the Defence, and as soon as we informed them yesterday that the Defence would like to use the ICTY wing and not the OTP wing, they immediately reacted and they booked the dates. So if the Defence follows formally up with a request to ICTY, then that could be accommodated. At the same time, we gave the Defence an address of the war crimes registry, the local registry in Sarajevo, who have proper offices, and the person in charge responded, and I passed the details to the Defence, that they're happy to accommodate the Defence in their offices as well. So there is lots of options for the Defence which they have to follow-up now formally, and again I think we have acted very, very swiftly as soon as we were informed. I don't know what channels the Defence used prior to that, to whom they talked, they did not talk to the Sarajevo field office and they did not talk to OTP before making that oral motion yesterday. My feeling is that there is absolutely no problem in accommodating these specific and legitimate requests by the Defence, but that's just what I can offer to the Defence and you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, this is all the mail that Defence has made regarding this problem, it's a series of letters. First one dates back to June 5th, which is when we started doing something right after we decided not to call these witnesses to the -- here in The Hague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's to the Registrar, Mr. Petrov at OLAD, because for Defence it's our contact in order to contact the different sections. The Defence has a very hard time finding its way in this labyrinth, the administrative labyrinth of the Tribunal but obviously this is the right address. After this we contacted the SS -- an SS department, I believe that's what it's called, and we were told a very bold answer saying it's not possible, which is why we decided to call on the Bench to help us out. And as of -- as soon as we asked for the Bench to help us out, things started moving. But I just wanted to show you that we did do a lot of steps before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's one thing I don't understand. I see that there are two wings in the Sarajevo field office, that's what Mr. Waespi -- Mr. Waespi said. Obviously you wanted to use the ICTY wing and not the OTP wing, which is normal. If there is an ICTY wing, that's where you should go and the green light shouldn't come from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then you said we were answered it wasn't possible, but what isn't possible? You were not allowed to use the premises or you were not -- are those the other facilities that you were asking for witnesses that was not possible? But what facilities are we talking about exactly? Transportation? Accommodation? I don't really understand what was not possible. There are two problems. On the one hand you've got the premises and then you've got the other facilities, but you did not tell us exactly which other facilities you were requesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Honourable Judges, in this first letter sent to Mr. Petrov, which was the person at registry that was in charge, we explained that we needed the premises, we needed a printer; and secondly, we needed to make sure that the witnesses would be there at the scheduled day and time, either in Sarajevo -- and we made a whole schedule for the Witnesses and Victims Section. Of course we don't have a lot of time available. I have to move over there, and Mr. Tapuskovic needs me here in The Hague. So we put aside three days all together for this trip -- or four days all together, because there's a morning included, for the whole trip, the trip, the work over there, and coming back. We obtained an answer on June 18th, and the last answer was very curt. It's -- came from the CMSS department telling us -- well, that's what we -- saying that the hierarchy of CMSS had told this person that it wouldn't be possible and that registry had nothing to do with the problem that Defence could have. Basically, the answer we got that it was our problem and that they were only there to certify things once the Bench has accepted the statements after the entire procedure that the Prosecution goes through. So for almost two weeks we tried to find a solution, and finally we called on the Bench. Maybe it's procedure but it does have to do with substance. I mean, there is Rule -- Article 21, paragraph 4 of the Statute of this Tribunal, equality of arms and fairness of the trial requires that Defence be helped in what it needs to do. Defence has less than Prosecution de facto, that's the way it is. Even in my own national jurisdiction, the Prosecution depends from the state and has maybe more resources, but we -- that's why we asked the Bench for this help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand now what happened. The Witnesses and Victims Section is telling you that if -- bringing the witnesses here in The Hague, that's okay, but collecting a statement, this is still investigation, and then that's Defence, that's Defence's business. Is that what they're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to tell you the truth, we did not obtain a direct answer from this department, from CMSS. We obtained a -- a comprehensive answer from the CMSS department encompassing all departments in registry, saying it was not up to them to help Defence in the steps it had to do. And these are our witnesses. We're no longer in the investigation process. The investigation process is over, but we did not collect written statements because we were not -- we didn't have to do that during the preliminary procedure, we were not supposed to collect these written statements. And unofficially we were told to do this, to collect the statements anywhere in bars, restaurants, or whatever, and I believe it was not very proper. You know, you can't really contact anyone to talk about a specific case in a bar, in a restaurant. I mean, the French law is extremely strict in this respect; you cannot do this. You have to bring the witness to some decent place to for the statement. Maybe I could ask them to come to my law office in Paris, but that would cost too much money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the court deputy to bring this matter to the attention of the Registrar and to report to us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next matter I wish to raise is a motion filed by the Office of the Prosecutor -- let's move into private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration again in open session. It's a formality, but one that's very important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the usher can show the paper now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document under seal as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as D247 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first I'd like to hear some background information concerning the witness, and if I may I'd like to ask for private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you have anything to do with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what sort of a relationship was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 13th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you know of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a separation line established between the Army of Republika Srpska and the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my case, on the 12th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly look at the map 65 ter document number 02829.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on this map can you indicate the separation line at which you were, as you said a moment ago, on the 12th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around here, but this is a very small map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. On the 12th of September, look at the two lines, the yellow and the red one. Where were you on the 12th of September, 1992? Where were your positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my settlement, below here. That was the line on the 12th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the line that was established and that survived throughout the entire conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In which brigade were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those yellow and red lines represent? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in the course of the conflict, as you were at the separation line, where the line held by the Ilidza Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, show us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's as far as I know. Nedzarici. I don't know about the other part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the please use another colour to indicate the line where you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 12th of September or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you where you were at the separation line throughout the entire conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first line was on the 12th of September, when we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you when the lines were established definitely. When were the lines established definitely? That's the line I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you adjoining another brigade towards the north?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer; the interpreter did not hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer. The interpreter did not hear the answer. Please repeat it, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again the interpreter did not hear. Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, again your answer was not heard. Please speak into the microphone, speak into the microphone, and repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Rajlovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw the lines where the Rajlovac Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know any more than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you can't see the end of the position where you were. You've drawn a line all around Nedzarici, but can you indicate where your position ended towards Nedzarici. Could you just make a dash across the line to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please explain to Their Honours the place where you were and its relative position compared to the other geographical features in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were in a valley, and as there were mountains on all sides, these were held by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not enough to say that. Can you say what mountains those were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sokolje, Zuc, Mojmilo, Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this map be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, excuse me a minute, I have a question, a clarification I would like to ask from the witness. Witness, you joined the army, the Army of the Republika Srpska, on the September 12th, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Well, how long did you actually stay and what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the end of the conflict. I did not have any rank. I was just a private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you. This will be my last question. The positions that you have just shown us, did they remain stable from September 12th, 1992, all the way until you left the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will be admitted as -- sorry for the interruption. The map will be admitted as D248.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the map disappears off the screen, can you tell us the following: The line you drew where you were throughout the war, where was it in relation to the house you lived in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it actually passed through the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw the place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, evidently we misunderstand one another. I'll ask you about this later on, but my question now was: This line where you found yourself at a certain point in time and which was the final and definite separation line, in relation to your house, where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking about the first conflict that occurred? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you when the lines that you have just drawn became established definitely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, those here, and those others on the 13th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's where the misunderstanding lies. And now I'm asking you once again: What was there on these lines? What was your geographical position when on the 5th of December you arrived at the positions you marked here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in a subordinate position because there were mountains all around, as I said, Sokolje. We had a refrigerator truck in front, there were railway tracks, and then an embankment some 10 or 15 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you explain now or explain to the Judges what happened before the 5th of December when those definite positions were taken up, what happened around your house and in that area before the 5th of December from the beginning of that year? Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an attack by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, seven or eight relatives of mine were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, time has its course. You mentioned the 5th of December and you mentioned the 12th of September. I'm asking you to explain first what happened before the 12th of September from the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was practically no war then. We were in our neighbourhood. We all lived there together, Serbs and Croats. We had guards -- held guard together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've already marked this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at map 65 ter 2872. If this eastern side could be enlarged, or rather, the western side, sorry. Could we zoom-in on the west side. A little more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now mark the place where you lived, where your house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can this be done in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Yes. In private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we see DD002523, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the B/C/S text is a bit unclear, but could you please carefully read the heading to Their Honours, first the heading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Command of the 102nd Motorised Brigade, Sarajevo, the 18th of September, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please read the introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could that be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Based on the situation on the ground and in connection with the Hladnjaca, cold storage depot, facility and large number of people" -- I can't really see what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to try hard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Through this important facility and in order to make it operational, it is important to use this facility in a planned manner. To that effect I hereby order: "1. That the cool storage facility be used exclusively for sniper nests as an observation post and firing positions of some weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the facility from which you said that they fired day and night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that's the facility that you could see very well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this into evidence as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown DD002529.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read as slowly as possible first the heading and then what follows underneath, and then all the way up until item 1, and the entire item 1. Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Sachdeva wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, as the Prosecution had done in their case, I think it would be proper for the -- for counsel to ask the witness first whether he has seen this document, whether he has read this document before, whether he has been involved in the drafting of this document, and then proceed on further questions, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you should certainly establish the provenance of the document and any relationship that the witness has with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I showed previously a document to the witness and this second document stems from the first document. The witness told you that from the cold storage facility they fired day and night. The second document speaks precisely of night shooting with the night-sights. The witness spoke about having experienced this. He certainly didn't draw-up this document himself. This is a document coming from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but even before I showed the first document to the witness he said that from the cold storage facility they opened sniper fire day and night. This second document will precisely support what the witness said; namely, that he has experienced this, as did people who were down there on the positions with him. The witness spoke about the cold storage facility, and now this document speaks about the fact that they opened fire during night from weapons equipped with night-sights. It says here in the document that these weapons have to be used 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, at least from the English there -- it appears to me there is no indication that this document relates to the cold storage facility, number one; and number two this is from the 5th of March, 1993, the previous document was the 12th of September 1993. So I don't see that there is a natural sequence in these two documents. And maybe it's for the witness to comment on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The dates don't suggest a sequence, a relationship. Is the witness in a position to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you answer this question. What you said about there being fire round the clock, did that continue throughout the time when you served as a soldier, until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the 5th of December until the end of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So there was firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was firing, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hence, I believe that this witness is somebody who can read out this document because this is his personal experience, and he can tell you about the consequences of this constant round the clock shooting and the victims throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question you wish to ask him about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to ask him whether everything he said is in accordance with item 1 here. I will read it out, if I may, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I hereby order: "Engage all brigade snipers permanently, in all weather conditions when possible. Weapons equipped with night-sights must be in use round the clock."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is this consistent with what you experienced during the war with those two facilities that we mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that this document be admitted into evidence as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I respectfully object to the admission of this document into evidence. I do not, I submit, think that the witness has established a connection with his testimony on this document, and he has not been able to comment at all on the provenance of this document. In fact, I believe it's the Prosecution's position that we would not object to this document being tendered, but appropriately so through a witness that can speak to it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, why don't you ask the witness to elaborate on the provisions of that first paragraph: "Engage all brigade snipers permanently in all weather conditions ..." Could he give some examples for -- that might assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was going to be my next question. Can the witness tell us something; namely, given what he said about there being fire round the clock, could the witness tell us something about civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was fire non-stop. We lost about 20 soldiers and civilians who walked by -- on the road by the school going to the market and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What period of time was this? What month and year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 5th of December throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What brigade are you talking about that was engaged in this -- in this action, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ilidza Brigada, the one where I was. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the 1st or the 2nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly don't understand your question. Which brigade? Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this order says: "Engage all brigade snipers," referring to all brigades. This order refers to all brigades and that's what it says in item 1. And then below this it says: "The snipers" -- it says here: "All snipers in possession of all brigades," so the order was issued to all brigades by the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, I think -- we are a little confused. The document is headed: "Armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, command of the 2nd Motorised Brigade," it is signed by "Safet Zajko," the commander, and the heading is: "More effective engagement of snipers." What snipers? Snipers belonging to whom? His snipers or snipers of the other side? That's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know in which language it is not clear. The only language that I speak, the B/C/S language, is clear as can be. It is an order of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina where it says very clearly the following: "In order to organise fire in a more planned, organised, efficient, and concentrated manner and make your available forces more deadly, I hereby order: " ... All brigades of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to engage all brigade snipers permanently in all weather conditions when possible. Weapons equipped," and I highlight this, "weapons equipped with night-sights must be in use round the clock." This is the order of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which pertains to brigades. In the previous document which spoke of a cold storage facility you were able to see a location from which they fired. I understand your hesitation, but this is a document that cannot be contested in any way but it explains what the witness said. This is a document that the witness is not familiar with; this is a document that I obtained from the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They did not have such evidence in the Galic case, and now we're offering these pieces of evidence which did not exist at the time of the Galic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The real problem is with the word "engage."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The difficulty the Chamber is having is that the English version of your document does not reflect that the order is addressed to all brigades; it only reflects that the order is addressed to the snipers of the 2nd Motorised Brigade of the ABiH, hence the confusion. Because we thought that if the area in which the witness was operating was the area that fell under the previous document; namely, the 102nd Motorised Brigade, then the Chamber had a difficulty in understanding why suddenly the snipers of the 2nd Motorised Brigade, which we thought was positioned somewhere else, was brought into the picture. But maybe the interpretation can clarify the issue by verifying the translation of the order in paragraph 1. Does it say: "Engage all brigade snipers permanently ..."? Or does it say: "Engage all the snipers in all the brigades ..."? I don't know if the interpreters can help us out here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that it says: "All snipers in possession of brigades" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are listening to the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We repeat: "All snipers in possession of brigades," is literal translation of the text. This is item 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what is the -- the translation of the word which we have in English "engage"? I'm asking the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It says: "All snipers in possession of brigades to be placed in permanent use in all weather conditions whenever possible." This is sentence 1 of item 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was right. The problem is "engage." Mr. Sachdeva, what's your understanding of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: My understanding now that the interpreters have sought to clarify is that, firstly, the -- the word "engage" is not contained in the B/C/S version, in the original version; secondly, that, in my submission, it would be -- it would not be the case that a brigade commander would be issuing an order to all brigades for snipers, if indeed they were in those brigades, to be at the ready. And with respect to the admission, I still assume my objection in that it is -- pre-dates the indictment, it pre-dates the crimes that the accused is charged for. The witness has not been able to establish a connection to this document from his testimony, in my submission. And thirdly -- well, those two submissions in terms of the objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tapuskovic, and then we'll rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something. This has to do with night shooting, that's the first aspect. Secondly, I'm certainly not going to testify here before you, I do not wish to do that, but the 2nd Brigade later on became 102nd Brigade. This is what it was renamed later. What is important, though, is that both of those brigades were constantly positioned at Stup which was right above the heads of this witness and other soldiers, but I don't want to testify about that. I think it is sufficient to note that this witness said what happened from the cold storage facility and that he said that there was night firing from weapons which were equipped with night-sights. This witness is just a private. Naturally, he has nothing to do with this document. He had never seen it before. He didn't draft it or have any contact with it. The essence is that there was firing from the cold storage facility throughout the war. Now we heard that there was shooting at night and that people, civilians, were killed in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D251, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have to ask you something else to try and clear up some matters before the Chamber. You said that until the 12th of September, 1992, the separation line went through your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the final separation line at which you spent the whole war was established on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me and explain what happened between the 12th of September and the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was sporadic fire and fighting until we reached the final position. My settlement was also shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which brigade did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Borislav Berjan platoon commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of orders did you receive? First of all, in what form, in writing or orally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Orally, over the radio or by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did they contain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stated that we should not open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "not open fire"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to fire as little as possible, to preserve ammunition since we were short of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What period was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1993 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was firing in 1992, from September until December, and then there was a lull. We only returned fire when they opened fire at us or when we were able to observe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you were able to observe them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were in the trenches, their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What could you see from those trenches in relation to the layout?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few roofs, a few demolished houses, that's it, and the cold storage plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where does the Miljacka go in relation to your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between us and the Rajlovac Brigade; it separated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, were you able to observe something in the Miljacka itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of April 1992, we would come across corpses and we would collect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was happening? What did you do with them and did it continue throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from 1992 until 1995. And those corpses would float down the river from the direction of the city, the city of Sarajevo which was controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where does the Miljacka go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to reach your positions in Ilidza, where was its bed? How did it -- where did it run?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is Sarajevo in your terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ilidza, Vogosca, all of it, but it goes through the very centre of Sarajevo and Skenderija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How often did that happen and what did you do with the corpses you pulled out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken to the Lakovo [phoen] cemetery and buried; subsequently, they were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to find out who those people were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a case in which people were trying to do something else with the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of 1994, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims used the Miljacka to leave the city. They used its bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of such a case in 1994 when something happened with those people who tried to escape that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A number of them were killed when trying to leave. There was a lady doctor; I personally pulled her out of the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did you find her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She had a back-pack, she was swimming down the Miljacka trying to reach us, and she was shot at from the direction of the railway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what her name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Maja, although I'm not sure. She left with her husband, who was wounded as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After he was wounded, where was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, when he got wounded, where was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We took him to the Zica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic assumed command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think sometime in 1994, although I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me anything about the fighting, the combat operations? What did they look like in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1994, it was truce. The only thing that was going on was sniping, but otherwise it was calm. But that lasted until November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of a weapon did you have, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, did you see some other weapons in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were in Ilidza. There were some tanks and Pragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like towards the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't see that at that time because they were under the control of the IFOR or whatever their name was, the UN in any case. It was all under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in November? What did it mean for your positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an all-out attack by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from all directions, Trnovo the most and the environs. It lasted in November and December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could one feel it in Ilidza as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was bombardment and shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From what direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Hrasnica the most, Hrasnica and Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a tunnel which existed there, since you mentioned Butmir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know of it. It has to do with the runway at the airport. At that point in time, I could move to an observation post from which we could follow what was going on with the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to observe anything concerning troop movements, and please take it slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was constant movement of the troops, from the city and back, and they were attacking us from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It began in November. When did it cease or when did it stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By February, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then there was a lull again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say "again," but please put it in a temporal context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six months in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened after those five or six months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again there were attacks by the Muslims or the Army of B&H.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did it mean to you at the positions where you were in Ilidza and in Stup and Hum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shelling went on incessantly, and they were not targeting troops as much as they did civilians. There was shelling of the settlement all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately how many casualties were there among soldiers and civilians in the area where you spent the entire war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Particularly during the all-out offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 or 15 soldiers and around 20 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness T-2. My name is Manoj Sachdeva and I'm a lawyer for the Prosecution and I'm going to ask you a few questions this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask just to start off with for Defence Exhibit 250 to be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you remember we -- you were answering questions about this document to Defence counsel. You remember giving evidence about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, would you not, that -- that nowhere in this document does it state that civilians are supposed to be engaged by snipers, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the cold storage plant, from what I could see, both soldiers and civilians were targeted from there .

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you, I'm asking you to simply refer to this document and to confirm that on this document there is no mention of targeting of civilians. You agree with me, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I ask for the next document to be brought up, that's D251.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Witness, it takes a bit of time. And you also remember giving evidence about this document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want to ask you the same question, that you would agree with me that there is no mention of engaging of civilians by snipers in this document. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the text, but from what I could see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But not -- but not on this document. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not according to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you remember answering questions from counsel about -- about -- I'll just get that. One second. Yes. Counsel was asking you about your evidence that there was fire round the clock, and you answered: "Yes, there was fire non-stop. We lost about 20 soldiers and civilians who walked by the road going to the school and market and elsewhere." Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you spoke about the civilians, can you tell the Court a date where you know of a civilian being targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you give me the name of the civilian that you know of being targeted by snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, children, Mladen Stjepanovic and Igor, I can't recall his last name. They were my neighbours attending the primary school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you saw them being targeted. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And where were they when they were targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother-in-law has a house close to the school. That was the route. It happened 30 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you see that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where did the shots come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only direction possible was from the cold storage plant, it was the only place from which they could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You don't know that it came from there, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most likely it wasn't from the direction of the school. It was from the direction of the plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Which year was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. April, May, June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you're not sure if it's in April or May or June. Did -- was this reported to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When was it reported to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right away, as soon as it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who reported it to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command of my company did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And which person in the command of your company did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Borislav Berjan, or the officer on duty. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You don't know who reported it to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you have the document or do you have the report that was given to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Before you gave testimony today, did you inform Defence counsel about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you tell the Defence counsel that you -- that this was reported and that there would have been a record of this offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And these civilians were -- you were close to these civilians, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say -- when I say you were, I mean you and your fellow soldiers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was. We were repairing my mother-in-law's house which had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you also spoke about the confrontation lines. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I could go back to I believe it's map 249, D249.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I understand, Witness, that the line where you've written the "C" is the line where you were positioned. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on the 12th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But it is not your evidence that on the 12th of September, 1992, the area just across from that line towards the bottom of the page was ABiH territory. That's not what you're saying, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try and take this slowly. You see the line there. You've just drawn a line and you've got the letter "C" on top of that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I understand that that is a line that you say was the confrontation line on the 12th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you see just across from that line towards the bottom of the page, I believe that the word is there Doglodi. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what I'm asking you is that area, and in fact the area beyond that, that was VRS territory, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I ask you with a pen just to write the letters VRS there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. I think there's been a misunderstanding, but just to the other side of that line that was also VRS territory, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that that area beyond that line is ABiH territory? Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has already explained very well. VRS was above that line, and he's already said that. He can continue answering questions now, but the area up there was VRS territory. I would like the witness to be asked precise questions to avoid introducing unnecessary confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to that line where the C is marked, will you mark the area that was under the control of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of Republika Srpska. That's what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the other side of the line, who was in control of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could ask for the map -- I think it was the first map the Defence had the witness mark, D248, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was this map discussed in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The one that was just on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the last map, that was the one that was discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I believe it was. My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic should have brought this to our attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the result that no -- no damage has been done, no prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could have -- that's it. This is the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you remember marking this map earlier on today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And -- well, firstly, the red line -- you see the red line there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see that the red line depicts the VRS confrontation line. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you agree with the fact that everything beyond that red line is VRS territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you about the AOR of the Ilidza Brigade - and we'll keep this map here for that purpose - but I want to just confirm with you that the commander of the brigade from 1993 at least until the end of the war was Vladimir Radojcic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's right that prior to his tenure as commander, the commander was a person called Pero Despojevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Despotovic, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who was the commander in the beginning of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All know is that his last name was Borovina and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the Ilidza Brigade, how many battalions were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you know that there was a 1st and a 4th Battalion. You know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I belonged to the 1st. I haven't heard of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the 1st Battalion, as you've indicated on the map, had Nedzarici in its area of responsibility. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what battalion they were. I know only about my own. I never went to Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you have drawn on the blue line -- you see that you've drawn with the blue line the area of Nedzarici within the Ilidza Brigade. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So there was a battalion within the Ilidza Brigade in Nedzarici. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I circled this only as Serb territory under the Army of Republika Srpska, but as for the battalion I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, my question was not about the battalion. Counsel asked you to identify the area of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade, and you did that with the blue line. So my question is this: That there would have been a battalion within the area called Nedzarici which is within the Ilidza Brigade. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know they held Kasindol and down here I circled that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in Nedzarici there was a barracks there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at that barracks there were weapons of the Ilidza Brigade. Isn't that also right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was never in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You also know that the Institute of the Blind was in Nedzarici. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before the war. I knew about it before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the war the Institute of the Blind was within the VRS area of responsibility, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I never went to Nedzarici during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you have drawn here the AOR of the Ilidza Brigade, and you can see from the map that the Ilidza Brigade controlled Nedzarici. Do you agree with me with what you've drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you have also just said that the Institute for the Blind was in Nedzarici. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it goes through there, but I can't pin-point within 10 or 15 metres which bit belonged to the Serbs or the Muslims because I was never there during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But in your time with the Ilidza Brigade, you -- as you said, you were in communication with your commanders of the battalion through radio and telephone. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only with the company commander, I as a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that you have never -- you have no information as to whether the Institute for the Blind was under VRS territory in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what about the School of Theology, which was also in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know where that is, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Maybe I can help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I can ask for Prosecution Exhibit 304 to be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, before I ask you some further questions, when you met with Defence counsel you explained to Defence counsel the -- the extent of your knowledge. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also -- in doing that, you also explained to Defence counsel that you would be conversant with the information regarding the confrontation lines within the Ilidza Brigade. Isn't that also right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, where I was, not the entire zone, not the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also told counsel that you would be conversant with the weaponry that the Ilidza Brigade had. Isn't that also right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only what I saw. Of course I couldn't see all the weapons in the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, of course you would agree with me that you don't have to see a weapon to know what weapons exist. Isn't that right? You can see requests, you can see -- you can have information from your colleagues, you can have information from your company commander. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was just an ordinary private. Nobody told me about weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try and help you now with respect to the Institute for the Blind. Now, you see where there is a red line with the letter "B." You see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know that that red line is -- runs along the road called Lukavica Cesta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that road is in ABiH territory, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see those arrows there pointing towards the letter "B," you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And those arrows emanate from the area of Nedzarici. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that area of Nedzarici was controlled by the VRS, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that road, the road that you just spoke about, the Lukavica Cesta, you must have heard during your time with the Ilidza Brigade that that road was known as the road of death. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know that Nedzarici was called the positions of death, but I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps Nedzarici was called the positions of death because it was from there that the SRK soldiers would snipe at civilians taking that road, the Lukavica Cesta. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. They were killed there every day, 10, 20 men, that's what I heard, because there were buildings overlooking them and they were sniped at. Mojmilo was higher up and they were shot at with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when you say "they were shot at," you are referring to the SRK soldiers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's correct that when they were shot at, as you have earlier testified, they would return fire. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For the most part -- first of all, it was snipers non-stop. I heard that in Nedzarici both civilians and soldiers were being killed by snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you also said in evidence that when asked a question by counsel whether you were -- when you spoke to your company commander, do you remember that evidence, and you said to the Court that you were ordered not to fire. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the cross, or rather, throughout the examination-in-chief, the Defence never asked the witness anything about Nedzarici, and with reference to the line he drew around the places where he was at, his positions, I asked him to draw a line showing up to where he had been. He never mentioned Nedzarici once because he never managed to get to Nedzarici once during the war. I therefore fail to understand why he's being asked anything about Nedzarici, when his area of responsibility is where he explained it was, and he never mentioned Nedzarici once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason why I have -- and I tried to elicit that from the witness. The reason why I persisted in these questions was because -- and again in my submission this illustrates the insufficiency of the 65 ter summary. In the summary it clearly states that the witness will give evidence with respect to the confrontation line between the two warring parties within the zone of the Ilidza Brigade and Nedzarici is within the zone of the Ilidza Brigade. And that's the reason why I'm asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Where are you leading to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when counsel asked you about the orders that your company commander gave you with respect to firing, and you said: "Well, the order was to fire as little as possible," to preserve ammunition. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And then you also said that: "We only returned fire when they opened fire at us or when we were able to observe them." You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And presumably, these orders that you received were echoed throughout the other battalions and companies in the Ilidza Brigade. Is that right? In other words, they should fire only in retaliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear anybody say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when you have just given evidence that -- well, you've told the Court that you don't know anything about Nedzarici, but you've just given evidence that you heard that civilians and soldiers were killed in Nedzarici. So what are you saying? Are you saying that you know or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so you must have heard that soldiers from the SRK would fire rifles and sniping rifles at civilians within the ABiH territory. You must have heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you heard that soldiers in Nedzarici would fire from the Institute of the Blind into ABiH territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where the Institute for the Blind is, let alone that they fired from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You never heard that SRK -- the SRK army had soldiers at the Institute of the Blind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you never heard that the soldiers of the SRK were in the School of Theology? You never heard that either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the weapons, since you've told -- told us about some weapons that you had in Ilidza. It's correct, is it not, that the Ilidza Brigade had mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably. I didn't see the mortars. I told you about the two tanks and the Praga.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you also hear about the use of modified air-bombs in the period 1994 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that in 1994 some fighters of ours were trying this and they were killed somewhere near Trnovo and Treskavica then and never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And they were killed because these weapons, these modified air-bombs, were inaccurate weapons, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I know they were trying it out and they were killed; that's what we heard. And I never saw -- heard it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you never heard that they were used after that and they were fired into the -- into the city of Sarajevo from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document, Witness, and that is 65 ter 02483. Witness, you see a document on your screen and you can see that it emanates from the Ilidza Brigade command. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we go to the -- the second page, you would also see that this document is -- emanates from your commander, the brigade commander, Vladimir Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see his name there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you would agree that this is an authentic Ilidza Brigade document, SRK document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, but I don't know. It should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you can see there in the beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we go to the first page again. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You agree with me that it says in the beginning that: "According to the order of the SRK commander on the 18th of June..." the Ilidza Brigade that is, when they say "we," "launched an attack towards Stupska Petlja"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you agree that this is an offensive action, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also see down there on the list of ammunition that's requested, you will see the 2.000 bullets -- 2.000 pieces for a 7.9-millimetre sniper -- sniper bullets. Do you see that requested there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see the request in number 12 and 13 for the 450, 82-millimetre shells and the 120-millimetre mortar shells respectively. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And moving on to the next page -- no, actually, we can stick to this page in the B/C/S, please, if we can scroll down -- no, I apologise, it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You will see there, Witness, at item 23, you will see the request for an FAB aerial bomb, ten pieces. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here "auto bomb," a couple. I don't understand. "FAB auto bomb," that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I put to you that it says: "Avio-bomb, FAB, ten pieces." That's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The Ilidza Brigade did use aerial bombs, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Why would there be a request for aerial bombs if they were not intended for use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to ask Vladimir Radojcic that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your commander was a professional military man, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And he was fighting a war at this time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: He was a fighting a war at this time -- in fact, he was engaged in an offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would agree that as a professional military man and someone who was engaged in military action, the request that he would ask for -- these requests for ammunition would be genuine and serious requests, intending to use -- for intent to use these weapons. You would agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
