utterances.text: I really don't know that. You need to ask him that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P775, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I could now ask for 65 ter 03209, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is another document on the screen and this is dated the 1st of July, 1995, that is -- and the previous document was dated the 28th of June. And you will see that this emanates again from the Ilidza Brigade command. Do you see that at the top?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the interpreters made a mistake. I wrote down the first document, its date, and I wrote down the 18th of June, 1995, not the 28th of June. I don't know whether this is relevant in relation to other undisputed facts, but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it the 18th or the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The first one -- the one I just showed before was the 28th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you also look at this document and if you look at the next -- the last page, you'll also see that it is signed -- that it emanates from your commander, Vladimir Radojcic. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And similarly, you would agree that this is an authentic document from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the list, you will see at the first page, please. You would agree that the document -- the request inter alia is for 20.000, 7.9-millimetre bullets. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the request is also for 70.000 pieces of -- 70.000 bullets for 7.62-millimetre automatic and semi--automatic rifles. Do you see that, the first item?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you move to the next page, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You will see again at item 13 and 14 the request for 350, 82-millimetre mortars and 251, 120-millimetre mortars respectively. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at the bottom, number 22 and 23, it's clearly indicated there, is it not, that the request is for ten FAB 250 aerial bombs and five FAB 105 aerial bombs. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's clear, is it not, Witness, that the Ilidza Brigade was not lacking in ammunition or weapons. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only know about my own positions; namely, that we lacked ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you agree that this is a document requesting a substantial amount of ammunition for this brigade. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This is not much. I don't know why this is important. I don't see why this is a large quantity of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know what a FAB 250 aerial bomb can do, one bomb? Do you know what damage it can cause?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You must have heard of the TV building in Sarajevo. You know the TV building, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, but I also heard that it was the Muslims who placed an explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You did not hear that the TV building was hit by an aerial bomb, modified air-bomb, fired from SRK territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You don't know that the SRK command, in fact, congratulated its troops for hitting the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I put it to you that the SRK and the Ilidza Brigade were not lacking in ammunition and weapons and, in fact, used all these weapons that they requested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my position that that is not the case. I was there on the ground, you weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you're telling the Court that you know for a fact that these weapons weren't used by the Ilidza Brigade. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the Ilidza Brigade, at least to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me try and understand you. You are saying that the brigade that you are part of did not use these weapons? You know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was certainly so. I just said to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in fact your knowledge is quite limited, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just talking about my own situation, about what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, in fact, you don't know at all that the SRK soldiers at the Institute of the -- Institute for the Blind, you don't know if it's right they were not firing at civilians in the confrontation lines. You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P776, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I could ask for 65 ter 03309, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you know the area of Hrasnica, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard of Hrasnica, but I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know that Hrasnica is a residential area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is quite far from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's not what I asked. I'm asking you that you would agree that Hrasnica, whether it's far or close to Sarajevo, is a residential area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Similarly, you would agree that Sokolovic kolonija is also a residential area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the same question for Butmir, you also agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let me just start by asking you to confirm that this is another document from the Ilidza Infantry Brigade from the 21st of June, 1995. Do you see that at the top?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's written. I don't see it in the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see that it's a daily report and you see that it was sent to the SRK command at the forward command post to -- in Vogosca. You see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, but there's no stamp. I could have written this, so I'm not going to confirm anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I know that the -- the copy is not the best copy, but you can see -- on the left-hand side, you can see that it indicates that this came from Vladimir Radojcic, the commander of the Ilidza Brigade. You see that, don't you? I understand that it's not the best copy. I'm just putting to you that that's where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It just says this here. There is no stamp whatsoever, and you're telling me that this is authoritative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I didn't say it was authoritative. I'm asking you to confirm that this -- what's written here is the brigade commander, Vladimir Radojcic. You see that there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness, having seen signatures on documents, he already stated twice that he believed the documents to be authentic. I have no objection to having this document admitted, but what the witness is saying is that he does not believe this to be authentic, because he doesn't see the signature. In the two previous cases, he was able to confirm that, even though the documents were not familiar to him. And we had no objections either. We do not object to having this document admitted if my learned friend wishes that, but this witness cannot confirm the authenticity of this document if the signature is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just note that the previous two documents were -- they were in a similar fashion to this document, in that the top part where it says the document emanates from was not stamped and he confirmed the authenticity of those documents. So in my submission there's no discrepancy, no difference, between this document and the previous two documents, but anyway I'll proceed. Now, I'd like to move to the second page, please. And if it can be scrolled up. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in the second paragraph on this page you'll see where it's written: "We confined civilian population to shelters by artillery attacks ..." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I need to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, first tell me if you see that sentence. "Teritorije Vezali" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it says here that: "We confined civilian population to shelters by artillery attacks on chosen targets along the depth of enemy territory, especially in the area of responsibility of the 104 Mountain Brigade, that is in Hrasnica, Sokolovici kolonija, and Butmir." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's clear, is it not, Witness, that the Ilidza Brigade was firing artillery on areas where civilians were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I truly don't know that. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's possible. And you would also agree that the fact that this is contained in this report I suggest implies that the Ilidza Brigade knew that they were firing on civilians or on civilian areas. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. It's possible, but I'm not aware of that. I personally don't know that because we didn't see civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P777 [Realtime transcript read in error "776"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you started off by giving evidence about the -- the events that took place from April 1992 through to September 1992. You remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic. Not insisting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to verify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would agree, would you not, Witness, that prior to the onset of the conflict, Ilidza -- the municipality of Ilidza which you lived in contained all ethnicities, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the transcript, both of these last documents were admitted into evidence as 776, both 3209 and 3309 were admitted as 776 according to the transcript. This is what's confusing me and I ask that it be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They're both admitted. The court deputy will see that any correction that is needed is made. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I was asking you about the time-period just before the onset of the conflict, and in Ilidza municipality there were Croats, Bosniaks, Bosniak Muslims, and Serbs living together. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And before the conflict, they were living together in relative harmony. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And once the conflict started, a degree of suspicion came on between the different ethnicities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it is also right that at that time a decision was made to act upon an earlier decision to create the municipality of Ilidza -- to create the municipality of Ilidza to be a majority municipality with only Serbs living there. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you know that at that time where you were present and where you were living, you know that Muslims and non-Serbs were rounded up and detained in facilities such as Kasindol and such as the hospital. You heard of that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that -- about Kasindol.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You heard that the Energoinvest was also a facility where non-Serbs were detained and incarcerated. You heard that as well, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In fact, it's correct, is it not, that from that time-period non-Serbs, Muslims, and Croats were expelled from Ilidza municipality, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You know who Nedjeljko Prstojevic is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President of the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And he was, as you've just said, the president of the Ilidza municipality, he was an influential person in that municipality. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's also right that he was the main architect, one of the main architects, in that municipality for the expulsion of Muslims and other non-Serbs from Ilidza. That's also right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to play an intercept. The ter number is 03297.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to play an intercept, a recording, of a conversation, a conversation that Nedjeljko Prstojevic was a part of and then I want you to hear this, and then I'm going to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is not hearing. Should we start again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's too much noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, Witness, this is how it is. And you can just try and listen as carefully as possible. I would ask you to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There will be some noise, but you may be able to hear. Listen carefully. Let's start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you heard there, did you not, that there was discussion about expelling the Muslims from Ilidza? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Poorly. I may have understood 10 per cent of the entire conversation. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, we do have a B/C/S transcript that I could also show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's rather long, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It is long, and I wanted to play it for contextual reasons, but of course with the transcript we can go straight to the salient point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think you can if you wish to. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, whatever is written down we need to know by what means it was taken down. I've listened to this intercept before, and I was unable to understand much. In order for the transcript to be credible, it would have had to have been done by someone reliable. We need to know who did it and who authorised the transcript as such. We know nothing about that. We have a very poor recording and then a text of sorts. I have listened to this intercept before, and while doing so I wasn't able to grasp much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, Mr. Tapuskovic is raising arguments about the admissibility of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I anticipated what I appear -- what I believe to be an objection. I would say that this transcript has been authenticated by the participant Nedjeljko Prstojevic himself during his testimony as a Prosecution witness in the Krajisnik case and the intercept has been admitted as Exhibit P796 in that case. I understand it was on the 19th of July, 2005. And therefore, pursuant to Rule 89, the exhibit has been admitted in an earlier proceeding and the Trial Chamber is entitled to take judicial notice of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll take the break to digest this one. We'll consider it and we adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, what is the provision of the Rules on which you rely?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. In fact, I had before the break said Rule 89, and in fact in my submission that can apply, but particularly I'm speaking to Rule 94(B), judicial notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "At the request of the party or proprio motu, a Trial Chamber, after hearing the parties, may decide to take judicial notice of adjudicated facts or documentary evidence from other proceedings ... relating to matters at issue in the current proceedings." And you say this falls under the heading of adjudicated facts or documentary evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Documentary evidence, Mr. President. You would recall that prior to the commencement of trial the Prosecution filed a motion regarding exhibits United Nations reports that had been admitted into evidence in the Galic and the -- I understand the Galic and the Slobodan Milosevic case; in other words, they had been admitted, their authenticity had been verified, and on that basis under Rule 94(B) we ask for the admission of those documents and the Trial Chamber granted the Prosecution request. So in my submission this intercept which has been authenticated by the participant himself during live testimony in the Krajisnik case would fall under the same category. And I also submit that it is, indeed, relevant to the matters at hand in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Why it is relevant? It's relevant primarily because the Defence counsel, not just with this witness but with other witnesses, has been submitting that the onset of the conflict was started by the ABiH or by the Bosnian Muslims, and in that effort the municipalities were overrun -- the outer-lying municipalities were overrun by the Bosnian Muslims. And in our rebuttal we are putting to witnesses and to the Court that, in fact, those outer-lying municipalities were - I won't use the word cleansed - but non-Serbs were moved out forcibly from those municipalities. I accept that with regard to the case at hand, with regard to the charges the accused is -- has to meet, it is not strictly relevant. I agree with that. However, the Prosecution has been forced to lead this evidence or to put these propositions to the witnesses, given the fact that they have been permitted to -- or the Defence has been permitted to lead this type of evidence with every witness that they have brought here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why did you refer to the Trial Chamber's earlier ruling? You say that this requests is on all fours with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The earlier ruling, that was at the commencement of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I refer to that with respect to the provision Rule 94(B), in that the Prosecution had asked for documents -- UN documents that had been admitted in the Galic proceeding and also of the Slobodan Milosevic proceeding, and under that rule we asked for these documents to be given judicial notice and admitted into evidence, and the ruling was in our favour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Prosecutor, wouldn't it suffice for the Chamber to accept the fact that these areas were in the end under the control of the SRK? Do we need to lead or to accept evidence as to why this happened? I mean, the end result is clear I think and is probably not disputed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, I agree with that; however, the Defence have themselves made an issue as to how these areas became under SRK control. And in the Prosecution's -- the Prosecution's position is that that is, indeed, not how the events progressed. And in fact, those outer-lying municipalities were deliberately -- the non-Serbs were deliberately moved out of those areas. But I -- the Prosecution agrees, and we have, in fact, from the very beginning of the Defence case reiterated our position that these facts do not impact on the guilt or innocence of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd rather not go into all of the matters touched upon by Mr. Sachdeva. First of all, there was no mention here of who persecuted who and it is not encompassed by the indictment. We have been saying all the while, though, that the entire population of those areas were affected by it, the people of Sarajevo, and we've tried to explain what Sarajevo is. They were affected in various ways and we have tried to explain how civilians were affected on both sides, in the general chaos that existed. Concerning persecutions of any sort, well I -- we think there were none, apart from the things that happened in such a chaos in Sarajevo is quite specific. I wouldn't dwell on that any further. Rather what is of importance is something else. In the Krajisnik case and in the Milosevic case, one of them, of course, was not completed due to the passing away of the accused; and as for the other, we only have the trial judgement for the time being. As Defence counsel, I tried to object to the authenticity of this document, and Mr. Sachdeva himself mentioned Rule 89. Such a document, as the one we had before us, falls precisely under Rule 89(D): "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." It is precisely this document, or rather, this intercept, something which falls under that provision with regard of the facts I've tried to explain to the Chamber. The way presented by the Prosecutor, strictly speaking and according to this Rule, this document may not be admitted, first and foremost because of the wording of the Rule; and second of all, neither of the cases referred to have been completed. That is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the -- the prejudicial effect which is -- that you -- you cite in relation to 89(D)? What is the -- what would be the prejudicial effect of admitting this document? Or, to put it another way, what is the issue of fairness that becomes relevant in considering this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document has not been forwarded to us in a way for us to be able to have a position on its essence. To be honest, I listened to the tape before, and I can't tell you anything, or I can't decipher a single fact that would have to do with this case. I see no connection with this testimony and this case, particularly so since the date is the 14th of June, 1992. At that time, we submit, the lines of defence had not been defined. According to certain witnesses that we are to hear, these were formed significantly later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The other point that you make is that the judgement from which -- or the decision from which this documentary evidence comes is not final in that it's on appeal. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that is one of the requirements for the -- for judicial notice to be taken, under 94(B)? That's your argument? Mr. Sachdeva, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, firstly, that from a strict statutory interpretation of 94(B) that is not a requirement that needs to have gone through a second-instance hearing or proceeding. It simply says: "Proceedings before -- other proceedings of the Tribunal relating to matters at issue."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The case on judicial notice establishes that quite clearly. In the decision that we gave, I recollect it to be in setting out the various factors, we identified that. And if I'm not mistaken, that may even have been commented on by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It -- it may -- it may refer to the facts that have been decided -- the facts that have been decided in a first-instance proceeding. But I submit that if a document has been admitted in a proceeding and -- one would not expect a document to be admitted in a proceeding of this Tribunal if its authenticity and provenance had not been established at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see, you're saying that the finality criterion only applies to adjudicated facts, not to documentary evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to give the decision tomorrow morning on this question of the admissibility of the transcript. So let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could ask for 65 ter 03298, please, to be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, before this document comes on the screen, you would agree that once the non-Serbs from Ilidza municipality were forcibly moved out of Ilidza, they were not allowed to return, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether they were forced to move out or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But they were not allowed to return, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the time of war operations, they probably did not. They were not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see a document now on your screen. It's from the -- the Republika Srpska Ilidza Serb municipality, the war commission, and you see Nedjeljko Prstojevic's name at the bottom. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see that the decision, at least the first sentence it reads: "The return of Muslims and Croats to the territory of Ilidza Serb municipality is forbidden for security reasons, as well as because the necessary conditions for their return do not exist. "With regard to that, crossing the border by Croats and Muslims in the direction of Ilidza municipality is also forbidden, unless they have written authorisation from the proper authorities." So I put it to you that this conforms with your evidence that they were not allowed to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were allowed to come back or not. I don't understand this document, really. Because Croats came to Ilidza throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When I asked you if -- I asked you -- or I put to you that they were not allowed to return and your answer to me was: "During the time of war operations they probably did not, they were not allowed to." And that answer conforms with this document, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because there was movement of weapons as well as people. For example, the people from Kiseljak that had to do with the HVO, therefore that had nothing to do with this. The Croatian army could enter Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you can read this document, and on this document there is no mention of the HVO or the ABiH. It speaks about Croats and Muslims returning to the territory, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm telling you what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- they came to Ilidza in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about -- I'm asking you what is written in this document, and in this document there is no mention of the HVO or the ABiH. It speaks only of the return of Muslims and Croats to Ilidza. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't understand this. I know there were both Muslims and Croats in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your previous answer when you answered the question and you said they were not allowed to return, are you changing that answer now? Is that what you're saying to the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not understand the question then. I do know, however, that Serbs, Croats, and Muslims lived together in Ilidza. Some may have left, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not talking about whether they lived together in Ilidza at that time. I'm simply putting to you that once the war started in 1993 and 1994 Croat and Muslim civilians were not allowed to return to the Serb majority municipality of Ilidza. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, in 1993 and 1994, some Croats were returning to my settlement. That's why I gave you the answer as I did. And as for this stated here that they were prohibited from coming back, I don't know about that. I know that some of them communicated with Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Kiseljak is not Ilidza, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P778, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have made your ruling; however, I object. I'd like to say that the witness rejected all of this. He said something quite to the contrary, which is that both Croats and Muslims came to Ilidza throughout the war. I will pose some questions of the witness of that nature later; however, the witness said that he knew nothing about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is right. The document is not to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having in mind the few last things you just said, can you tell us a few names, names of Croats who came to Ilidza throughout the war from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know their first names. I don't know their last names, but those people still are down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I guess it's not that important then, since this document was not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the Prosecution document to the witness, this being P776.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see this document before you, but first let me remind you. You said that the orders were to save up ammunition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Without going back to all of that, can you tell us what did it look like during the times of that offensive that summer, did you have sufficient ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the document now. What is the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 1st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've said already that this was a request to receive ammunition. What it says here about the 28th of June, does that correspond to what was happening during the offensive you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I read this to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To try and make it easier. Let's have a look at what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the 28th of June, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question because the witness has maintained in his evidence in chief and in cross-examination that he can only speak to events within his AOR, and that did not include Nedzarici and Stup, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document that was not authored by the witness and that he knows nothing about since he could not confirm its authenticity was introduced by the Prosecution exactly through this witness. He knows of the offensive, of the lack of ammunition. Therefore, I don't believe we can limit the right of Defence now to examine the witness on this document, particularly with a view of what is stated here, and that is that they suffered constant artillery and infantry fire by the enemy and that they were forced to defend themselves and to defend this object of considerable strategic importance. It cannot be irrelevant. We need to pursue this further with this witness which has already been confirmed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's not saying that it's irrelevant. He's saying that the witness had previously, in examination-in-chief and in cross-examination, confirmed that he could only speak with certainty about matters within his AOR. That is what -- AOR means area --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Area of responsibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Area of responsibility, and his AOR does not include Stup and Nedzarici. It's not a question of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand the issue at hand. However, the question was whether they did or did not have weapons. He said that there was no ammunition, and in that regard this is very important. This is a request for ammunition which was lacking, and it is stated why it was made, because the context was as described here. They asked for ammunition; whether they received it or not, I don't know. But it proves that they did not have sufficient quantities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness. What is the basis of any knowledge that you have about this matter in relation to Stup and Nedzarici, considering that it is outside your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about these events. All I know is that there was no ammunition at the time. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Move on, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same problem arises with another document that has been admitted into evidence, but I don't want to dwell on it, and that's document 776. I don't know whether that number still holds good or whether it's been given another number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ask the court deputy. Is that -- what's the number of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is P776.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. The previous document we found it under number P776, but the dates are different. Are they -- do they both have the same number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, my records show that 65 ter number 03209 was tendered and admitted as P776, followed by 65 ter number 03309, which was tendered and admitted as P777.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We follow the numbering given by the court deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, let's see document P777.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There you see there's mention here of certain actions linked to Hrasnica and the airport. You said that you observed troop movements below the airport and Hrasnica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There's also mention of Doglade, where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Doglade area is mentioned here, Doglada. Let the witness look at the date and reply, if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Under 1, can you read it. Is that what was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Should I read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The enemy -- during last night and today, the enemy carried out combat activities on our defence lines provoking from infantry weapons in the region of Doglade and combined artillery-infantry attack in the region of Nedzarici ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this correspond to what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, since the witness is about to leave, we thought it might be prudent if the Chamber could pronounce its decision on the issue that is pending; namely, on the admissibility of the transcripts of the conversation. And one issue which I did not understand fully was whether the -- whether the transcript was admitted into evidence in the Krajisnik trial and authenticated by one of the persons who spoke in the intercepts and who was called as a witness in Krajisnik. Is that correctly understood? In other words, Mr. Sachdeva, what is your basis for claiming that this has been authenticated?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the participant, Nedjeljko Prstojevic, testified in Krajisnik as a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did he confirm that he was speaking -- that it was his voice on the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I understand that he did, and I understand that he confirmed the contents of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you show us to any paragraph in the Krajisnik judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I -- the judgement -- I understand that it was admitted on the 19th of July, 2005, and that the exhibit is 795 and it was through Prstojevic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I understand that if -- if it has to be adjudicated, then I suppose it will have to be found somewhere in the judgement, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that is the case -- that that needs to be the case. With respect to -- with respect to documents or exhibits that have been admitted in an earlier proceeding, the supposition is that they have been authenticated in that proceeding. And therefore, in the interests of efficiency and time, these documents can be admitted again. And in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All you have to show is that the document was admitted in the earlier proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And in fact the -- I refer again to the -- to the precedent set by this Trial Chamber with respect to the documents that were admitted in Galic and Slobodan Milosevic, albeit the case did not finish. It is not the case that every single document that was admitted was mentioned in the judgement; however, the documents were authenticated in that proceeding and admitted on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In fact, I have here the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 24th of January this year on that issue, and in the relevant part it reads: "Considering that in order to take judicial notice of documents, the Trial Chamber must be satisfied that the documentary evidence for which notice is sought, A, was tendered and received as evidence in other proceedings." Then there is a footnote, footnote 4, in which is cited the Milutinovic case; Prosecutor versus Bizimungu et al., an ICTR case; and Prosecutor versus Nikolic, a decision of the Appeals Chamber on the 1st of April, 2005, paragraph 45, where the Appeals Chamber concurs with the Bizimungu Trial Chamber in concluding that documents do not need to be adjudicated, as is the case for facts for which judicial notice is sought. In other words, the Chamber in previous proceedings does not need to have pronounced a specific and unchallenged or unchallengeable decision on the contents of the document, simply to have admitted the document into evidence.". That's the end of footnote 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That supports the position taken by the Prosecutor, and the Chamber, by majority, will admit the document, that is, the transcript. Judge Harhoff is not satisfied as to its relevance. Judge Harhoff dissents. That means, therefore, that we should allow any questions -- did you have further questions on this or you were -- you just sought its admission? So the issue now is whether Mr. Tapuskovic has any questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I did put a question to the witness and the witness had told the Court that he was not able to -- I believe his answer was that he could only hear 10 per cent of the intercept. And therefore, the prospects of the transcript was raised -- of showing the witness the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see, so you want to show it to him now, show him the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, so he can see the transcript, and I can put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and to put particular passages in it to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let that be done. We should try to and get this witness out of here by the end of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it assists, although I understand the ruling has been made, I could provide the transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If it may assist, I understand a ruling has been made, but I can provide the transcript reference in Krajisnik when the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the intercept we heard, you told the Court you could only hear 10 per cent of that intercept. Now we have a transcript -- we have a transcript from that recording on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we could go to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we can go down -- if we can scroll further down, please, and on the English as well. Further down, please. We'll have to go to the next page. I'm sorry. Please scroll down. I think we have to go to the next page. I apologise. Okay. That's fine -- if you can go back up to the top. And I understand that's on the B/C/S that would also be page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you see now on the right-hand side of the screen you see where it says -- where it's recording Nedjeljko Prstojevic and it says: "Well, what should we do? Would it be good if we gave it a thought and if we organised people from outside to expel them all. Nobody needs to be shot or killed. Everyone expelled." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see it? And so my question after reading this transcript of a conversation that Prstojevic had, and has confirmed in a proceeding in this Tribunal, I put it to you that the non-Serbs, and the Muslims in particular, were expelled from Ilidza municipality in the early part of the conflict. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Anything on that, that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prstojevic, Nedjeljko Prstojevic was what, did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any military authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In whose name was he speaking, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, read what it says here. What -- "Well, what shall we do? Would it be good to give it some thought." When somebody says in our language "to give it some thought," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it can happen but maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, regarding this exhibit, 65 ter number 03297, the audio portion will be admitted as P778 and the transcript will be admitted as P779.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a request concerning D248. We marked something on the map and that was saved, then we added something, and I would like that to be saved also. I understand it is still within the computer's domain and is still able to be saved as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so, it's still within the computer's capability?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we saved it just in case Defence counsel wanted to tender it at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have been anticipated. Witness T-2, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it. You may now leave, but we are going to adjourn in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this exhibit is to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map with additional markings will be admitted as D252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And then we are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of June, 2007, at 2:15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.51 p.m.,
